utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. I call Hamdija Kahrimanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is that No. 30 listed on your new list, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Hamdija Kahrimanovic, 28, your Honour. 28 on the new list, 30 on the old list. HAMDIJA KAHRIMANOVIC, called

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, would you take that oath, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is your full name Hamdija Kahrimanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you born on the 6th February 1942?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in a locality called Kozarusa, between Kozarac and Prijedor, about 1,400 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you attend primary school in Kozarusa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Kozarusa I completed the first four grades, and in Kozarac another four.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After that I think you did secondary school in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I graduated from the Secondary School of Economics in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you then went to Belgrade where you attended Teachers College?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I went to Belgrade and graduated from the Teachers College in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Following graduation as a teacher, did you then go back to Kozarac to teach?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I graduated as a secondary school teacher. I went back to Kozarac after graduation and I found employment in the Rade Kondic elementary school in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Then did you in 1968 build a house in Kozarac where you lived until the commencement of the war in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During your time at the school in Kozarac did you serve part of the period or some considerable part of the period as the principal of that school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in 1974 I was appointed assistant principal and I remained in that post for just under two years. After that I was for two terms, that is for eight years, the principal of the school in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you do your military service in Macedonia from 1965 until 1966?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Macedonia, the towns of Tetovo and Gostivar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you by nationality and religion a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know the accused in these proceedings, Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: For how long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, as soon as I was employed in Kozarac I lived with my parents until about 1967. Then I moved in Kozarac. I lived in a building across the street from the school, a small apartment, studio, and about 15 or 20 metres away from Dule's parents until 1968 when I built my own house. Therefore, I know him a very, very long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was he ever a student at your school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he must have been a student of our school. I do not know exactly when he went to school, possibly the higher grades in '66, '67,'68, I do not know exactly when he was born, but since the school is there and all his brothers went to that school, then he must have gone to that school. I do not remember teaching him personally because while I was in the classroom I usually worked in the first shift, you see, but the rule of the school was that for students living in the immediate vicinity of the school to attend in the second shift, so it is possible that I replaced someone in the afternoons, but mostly I worked in the first shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know where Tadic lived in the town of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course I know. I could not go into the street or into my yard without seeing the building in which the Tadics lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you please look at Exhibit 196, if that could be shown to the witness? (Same handed to the witness) Mr. Kahrimanovic, I would ask you, first of all, to look at that document and can you tell me whether you recognise what it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the main road through Kozarac, the Marsala Tita Road going from Rajkovici to the Prijedor/Banja Luka junction. This rectangle indicates the Tadic house -----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If I just stop you there for a moment? I would ask that the plan be put on the overhead projector. We want to put it on the video screen beside you there, Mr. Kahrimanovic. I would ask you, if you would, just to point with a pointer, firstly, to where your house is, if you are able to identify that for us. You will need to do it on the screen beside you and to your right. You cannot do it on the television screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry. I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You will have to do it on the plan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This should be Tadic's house and in this part is my house. Somewhere here, going from Tadic's house to my street, it is the Prvomajska Street, and the second house on the right is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I ask you, if you would, to look at these two photographs that I now show you. Just have a look at these two photographs and if they can be marked respectively A and B, 237A and B, and then shown to the witness? Mr. Kahrimanovic, I would ask you to look at these photographs you are shown and if you recognise what it is a photograph of, could you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this photograph is the cafe owned by Dule.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: OK, and the other one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And this photograph is of his house which was built on top of the old house. The upper floor was his own apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you refer to "Dule" and his, are you referring to Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was usually known as "Dule" in Kozarac. Most frequently he was referred to as "Dule". It was his nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender those photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is 27A the cafe and 27B the photo of Mr. Tadic's house?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look at the back of the photograph for me, please, or perhaps just pass them to me? 27A is just the house and 237B is the cafe.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 237A and B will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you just put them on the screen firstly and zoom up on that, if you would? Just looking at that, Mr. Kahrimanovic, what is that? Can you describe that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the Tadic house. Below is the old building in which they used to live and the upper floor was built later, and that was his actual apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If you go to the right of the screen there, you see a building starting to project out from there in the photograph. Is that also part of the Tadics' building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is an annex and in that annex is the cafe, the business premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you look at the next photograph, 237B, and are you able to tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the cafe, that is the business premises, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps they could be returned to the Registrar? Mr. Kahrimanovic, this is the building that you would see, is it, from your house if you turned into your street and headed towards the main street of Kozarac? Mr. Kahrimanovic, if you walked into your street and turned towards the main street and walked up towards the main street of Kozarac, is that the building that you would see when you walked up towards the main street of Kozarac from your place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As far as you know, did Dule Tadic and members of his family live in these premises for all of their lives for all of the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not say because he probably spent a part of his life after elementary school studying somewhere and then he probably did his military service. So it is hard to say, yes, that he spent his whole life there. But recently, that is several years before the war, he lived there without interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know the names of his mother and father, Dule Tadic's mother and father?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. His father's name is Ostoja, his mother, Staka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is his father still alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he died a few years before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know his father?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew him well. He was a man of prestige. He was the bearer of the 1941 partisan badge. We are neighbours. We were very close. We must know each other. We had to see each other almost every day. But, you know, you are living in the same community and that is how it is in everyday life.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know whether Dule Tadic was married when you were living in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know his wife's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mira.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know where she worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most recently, the years before the war, she worked in the health clinic in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did your wife work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My wife also worked in the health clinic in Kozarac. This institution was the only one she worked in and continued working there. Her entire employment was there, first in the old building and then in the new one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did your wife stay in this employment up until the takeover of Prijedor in April/May 1992 when she was dismissed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the takeover in Prijedor she worked in the health clinic in Kozarac, and somewhere in mid-May 1992 she assessed the situation as it was and she left and went to Austria to stay with our son.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know whether Dule Tadic had any children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dule Tadic had two daughters. I am sorry, I did not answer the previous question you asked me. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think the answer you have given is sufficient. Did you know any of the neighbours of Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I knew them all. I knew all the inhabitants of Kozarac, but Dule Tadic's home was very much in the heart of Kozarac. It was surrounded with Muslim houses. If we go from the direction of Prijedor towards Mrakovica, there is Ankic Salih's house, then the house of Dule and Dule's parents, then Sulja Mujagic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think just on either side would be sufficient, if you can tell us that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Across the street, not exactly across the street but diagonally, is Hamdija Hodzic's house, then an apartment building socially owned in which teaches worked, lived, and next to it another socially owned building with a chemist shop, a barber's shop and above that were apartments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that is probably sufficient. Did you know from time to time whether Dule Tadic used premises at the school for the purposes of teaching karate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was then principal of the school when very often we met his requests and allowed him to use the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did students of the school from time to time attend his karate lessons in this hall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did. Members of the club were certainly students of our school and it was in our interests for our children to take part in sports, and karate is one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what Dule Tadic was trained as when he did his education, his schooling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After elementary school, eight year elementary school, I know he went to secondary school -- at least I heard it from his parents because we were often in touch -- but I do not exactly know what speciality he graduated in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know any of Tadic's friends that you saw him with from time to time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, he was often in the company of my colleagues from school, Kemal Susic, Basic Zijed, Sinanagic Mustafa. He was also friendly with others, but these boys were linked with him mainly through sports.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What sport in particular was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am thinking of karate and the colleagues I mentioned, they were teachers of physical education.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know whether Dule Tadic was in any way involved in politics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More recently, just before the war, it could be noticed that he was engaged in politics, but earlier on, I would not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember reading an article in a newspaper sometime in 1990, 1991, relating to Dule Tadic and his family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the nature of this article that you read in the newspaper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the article was published in a Belgrade newspaper called Vecernje Novine. The contents of the article could roughly be summarised as follows, that Dule Tadic had received an anonymous letter in Kozarac saying that if he does not move out within three months, he and his family would be liquidated, with an unclear signature of the author of the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know whether this matter was investigated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, that letter was like thunder because until then nothing like it had happened and the leading party in Kozarac reacted, disassociating itself from the text, from the letter and spirit of the letter. I know that an analysis of that text and the letter and the handwriting were investigated in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know whether the person who wrote the letter was ever discovered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not read the official report of the police regarding the analysis, but it was widespread, the rumour was widespread that the author of that letter was Mira Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you said the main party in Kozarac, the leading party in Kozarac, reacted disassociating itself, are you referring to the SDA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the ruling party at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Prior to this letter being published, had any incidents like this occurred in Kozarac that you can recall relating to tension between the ethnic groups in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was this article published in the newspaper in Belgrade as well as the local newspaper in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The article appeared in the Belgrade newspaper, but you know what journalists usually do, after such a sensational article then they copy the same context and that text appeared again in the Kozarac Vjesnik and in the daily newspaper of Oslobodjenje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why do you describe the article as being "sensational"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the locality of Kozarac, its inhabitants, did not deserve because they had not shown any reason for being humiliated in that way; to say that the people of Kozarac were threatening anyone with liquidation is something unacceptable because we were not like that, we, the people of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the SDS party and the Serbian people, Bosnian Serbian people, in the region who were associated with that Party rely on this letter in the course of their political campaigns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever see people involved in the SDS party gather at the premises of Dule Tadic while you were living in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, more recently, that is right before the war, Dule Tadic socialised with more or less the same circle of people in Kozarac. Let me mention, for instance, Milos Radulovic, Dusko Kesic, Mirko Grahovac, Trivo Relic, Slobodan Selimovic. Those were people who lived in that locality. Very many did not even live, had ceased to live, in the place itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were these people involved in the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my own view, all the Serbs in Kozarac were members of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mentioned one person, Simo Miskovic, do you know his involvement with the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Simo Miskovic was even the President of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: President where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the headquarters of the party was in Prijedor. I presumed they had their branches in surrounding localities such as the area of Kozarac, Omarska especially, that is, in those parts where there was Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from Tadic's premises, his cafe, do you know where else these meetings were held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Often times one could see, even I had the opportunity to see, often how groups of those people met in the priest's house in Kozarac which was almost next to the church in Kozarac. One could even observe them walking around Kozarac often, presumably, discussing whatever they had to discuss. Myself, I, for instance, saw Dusko Tadic with Djoko Kesic who worked as a laboratory technician in the health centre in Kozarac, and they would meet and then have their tete a tete, conversations. Some permanent premises, I mean, some local premises, fixed premises in Kozarac, I do not think existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you refer to "priest" you refer to the Serb orthodox priest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we called them "pop" like that, we just say "pop", priest. He is, of course, the Serb orthodox priest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from meetings that took place in the town of Kozarac and surrounding areas, were there meetings, to your knowledge, held in other towns in the opstina of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Frequent contacts, frequent meetings, took place in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Any particular reason why these meetings would take place in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My personal view, yes, Omarska was an exclusively Serb locality with Serb inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This time frame that we are talking about when you made these observations about these meetings in these various places of these people, is that the period 1991/92?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, especially '92.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In 1992, particularly leading towards April and May, did you and other members of the Kozarac community take steps to address the deteriorating political situation in the Kozarac region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the inhabitants of Kozarac, especially in May, during May '92, created a Citizens Peace Council, a Council for Peace Citizens League. I was one of the members of that forum. Members of this forum were mostly prominent inhabitants of Kozarac, people of prestige there, who thought that we should try to solve the problems that had already begun and appearing there by peaceful means and to try to continue as we did until that time. I remember that sometime in the middle of May we had a joint meeting of a part of that League of ours because we could not always meet in full because, of course, people worked, but sometime in mid May '92 we had a meeting in Prijedor which was attended by Dusko Tadic, among others. He was also involved in this patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from Dule Tadic and yourself, can you remember other members of this particular League of Peace?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you name some of those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr. Jusuf Pasic, Kemal Fazlic, Hamdija Balic, Kemal Susic, Husein Mujagic, Dusko Tadic, Milenko Zigic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Which of those people that you have named were Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic was a Serb and Milenko Zigic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know why Dusko Tadic was appointed to the League of Peace?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a very simple reason, that we wanted, because until that time we had lived together, to go on fighting for our joint life in the future, and we did not want only the Muslims turn out to be the only ones fighting for this joint life. We wanted, we cared about having other people, representatives of other ethnic origin on our forum in Kozarac, a Serb, for instance, who lived in Kozarac, because we did not want it to look like a mono-ethnic forum, mono-ethnic Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You speak of attending a meeting from Prijedor, that is, the League of Peace attending a meeting in Prijedor during May, do you remember mentioning that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In the middle of May we had a meeting in Prijedor and at that meeting the citizens, inhabitants, of Kozarac represented by me, by Dr. Jusuf Pasic, by Hamdija Balic, Kemal Susic, Dusko Tadic, Milenko Zigic. That meeting was also attended by delegates from the Local Commune of Kozarusa. I recall that they were represented, that delegation were represented, by Djuro Pupavac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who represented the people in Prijedor that you went to see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serb authorities were represented by Simo Drljaca, the MUP Secretary in Prijedor, and Simo Miskovic, President of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was discussed at this meeting and what was the outcome of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we deliberated about how all the inhabitants of the locality of Kozarac should be loyal to the Serb authorities because it had taken over the power on 30th April, whilst members of the police in Kozarac should also sign and write allegiance to the Serb authorities, that is, citizens of the locality of Kozarac should be invited to turn over their weapons. Those were the questions that our attention was riveted on. There were also some other questions. We were guaranteed that after we met all those conditions, no complicated situation or problems would arise. For instance, there was a question: Well, if no problems are going to arise, then why had Kozarac been left by the orthodox priest and gone to Omarska? And then we were charged with a task of trying to return the priest, the orthodox priest, to Kozarac, and Kemal, myself and Dusko Tadic were charged with trying to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What had happened to the orthodox priest in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know why, for what reason, he left the locality. Perhaps he was familiar with the situation and knew what the future held for Kozarac and Kozarac people. But due to the circumstances and the situation which was very tense, we met especially in May, we asked the orthodox priest to return to Kozarac and that the Kozarac inhabitants guarantee his safety and for those reasons we wanted, we were charged with trying to bring him back. However, we failed. We failed because all the three of us in a mission, Dule Tadic was made responsible to establish contact with the orthodox priest and then to arrange a meeting with him and convince him to come back. The next day when we had agreed to go to Omarska, Kemal Susic and I met in front of Dule's coffee bar and he told us that the priest could not receive us today, he was too busy. So we postponed our mission to the next day and the next day, the same story, the same answer. We would postpone it for the day after the next and Dule was gone by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you attended meetings in Prijedor where Simo Drljaca and Simo Miskovic were presiding, do you know what role, if any, Dule Tadic played in these meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we all had the same role, but we did not behave identically. Our common role was to find a common compromise, a peaceful solution. However, individual members of this Peace Council acted in a destructive way, nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you able to name any of the individual members of the Peace Council who had acted in a destructive way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, Dule Tadic, for instance; he had undertaken a responsibility probably just to meet the form. For Kozarac people, it was very important, it was fundamental, to have this orthodox priest of Kozarac living amongst us and to be safe there. He did not fulfil this undertaking, this mission -- for what reason he probably knows himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were ultimately the citizens of Kozarac given an ultimatum by the authorities in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That ultimatum was as follows. By May 24th, all citizens of Kozarac were to take -- turn down, turn over, sorry, their weapons by 12 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were they required to do anything else other than turn over their weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The police officers were to sign their allegiance, also turn down the weapons. Those were the central issues of the ultimatum, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was this ultimatum discussed with the citizens of Kozarac and was it acceptable to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, listen, after the discussions within that League of ours, we returned to Kozarac. We organised rallies, meetings, with people there and informed them about the contents of our discussions. I and other members of the League at a meeting of all the people of Kozarac were given the task of visiting larger urban communities in the area of Kozarac and talk to people directly. Specifically, I and Kemal Fazlic were given the task of attending a rally of the villages of Suhi Brod close to Kozarac on a route to Trnopolje. We talked to people but their reactions varied. Some were for and others against. People had been informed, were informed, about what had happened. Two people in the areas which had responded positively and laid down their weapons and they expected similar moves to be organised in Kozarac. So people behaved in different ways. But I know that some areas accepted the ultimatum such as, for instance, villages of Hrnici or Suhi Brod which did turn over their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But as a result of this partial rejection of the ultimatum, was Kozarac then attacked on Sunday 24th May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you stay in the vicinity of Kozarac until 26th May 1992 when you joined a group of people that had gathered in the street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in Kozarac. I did not want to leave it, whatever the cost. That Sunday, May 24th, all my neighbours, Fazlic family, Saric family, Kusuran family, we were all in the cellar of the family of Dautovic. They were all people who lived in my street. At 1.25 I saw the first shell hit my yard. From then on the shells became countless. It is true that on May 26th I joined the column of people moving from the direction of Mrakovica, that is, from the upper part of Kozarac. I asked them, "Where are you going then?" because that morning I had run out of the cellar and my neighbour had asked me, told me, "Hamdo, will you go up and see what is happening? We can hear some noise up there". So I asked the people where they were going, and they said, "We are going to the crossroads of the Banja Luka/Prijedor road". I returned to the shelter and I told my neighbours, "I am joining that column". I took the bag that I already had prepared and they followed suit, and that is how we joined them and headed towards Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At Kozarusa, were men and women separated from the group and were you placed on a vehicle that took you to the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from the Kozarac junction on the road Prijedor/Banja Luka, we moved perhaps a kilometre up to the bus station which we used to call Limenka, and we saw there masses of weapons, masses of military tanks, APCs, enormous quantities of them, and on that road the controls that took place, and women and children were taken to one side and men to the other. After the search and the control, we were boarded on to buses. Some people remained at that checkpoint, unfortunately, forever. I entered the bus where my neighbour Ilijaz, my neighbour Abdulah, my brother-in-law Zijad were already on that bus, and we were taken with many more people -- I cannot remember them all -- to the premises of the tiles factory called Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you spend the night of 26th at this camp and the next day, 27th May 1992, were you then taken to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on 26th we arrived in Keraterm, perhaps around 10.00 or 11.00. I cannot remember. We spent the night there. Then Wednesday came and we spent the whole day where we were. We were getting ready to go to sleep, and then around 9.00, 9.30 in the evening, somebody said, "Buses are arriving on the Keraterm grounds", and somebody, I think, even mentioned that there were 26 of them. A little bit after that, the gates opened, "Get up, in columns, one by one", and 70 on to each bus. We started on Wednesday around 2200 hours and arrived in Omarska between 3.00 or 4 o'clock in the morning and that was a journey of horror. You see, I mean, it was 20 kilometres only, yet you see how long it took. We stopped very often. People were taken off those buses. Bursts of fire could be heard. Buses crawled and, as I have said, we arrived in Omarska between 3.00 and 4.00. There we were taken by surprise because we immediately attended a very ugly scene when a man from Kozarac was beaten probably so that we could see what was in store for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were you taken to when you went to Omarska, where were you kept when you first arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They locked us in a hall. To be honest, Omarska is, well, near Kozarac, some 15 kilometres, yet I never been there. I have only been to the place, so that was my first encounter and a very ugly one. It was night time. I did not know the area at all, but the door of the bus, the front door opened right against the entrance into the room where they put us. Then this bus on which I was, those prisoners went into that room and then they continued coming and coming and coming. I do not know how many really, but I think about four or five hundred people were put in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see the accused Dule Tadic when you were in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see him once or on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did you first see him in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That Thursday when we arrived in the camp, I was in the second group of five taken for interrogation and after the interrogation we were taken back to a place which was called "garage" and there were very many of us there. Once I counted up to 150 and I did not go on. Then Friday came and since there were many, the garage door was open and we were let out of the garage pista. We were staying -- we were standing the length of the building which housed that garage. We stood there until late afternoon, until dusk. The sun had already set when we were taken to another room on the upper floor of that structure. We were allowed either to sit or to stand up, however one felt like doing. At a certain point I stood up because I was bored with sitting, I could not sit any more and, as I started standing up, I noticed, I saw Dule Tadic, and I turned suddenly my back and sat down and I did not stand up any more. Of course, I did not move until we moved to this other accommodation, to that room on the upper into.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was this the Friday after the attack that occurred on the previous Sunday, 24th May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So that would make it 29th May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At what time of the day, can you remember, did you see Dule Tadic, approximately what time of the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was the afternoon. I can hardly say what time of the day it was because without a watch one had to look at the sun to assess this, but I should say around 4.00 or 5.00 perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you recognise him when you first saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How far away from him would he have been when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, listen, some 20 or so, he was standing in front of the kitchen, in front of the canteen, well, listen, some 20, 25 metres. I would not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were the weather conditions like? Did the weather conditions in any way hamper you having a good view on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That day was very bright and sunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did anything else obstruct your view that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember that there was anything that could obstruct my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was Dule Tadic on his own when you saw him or was he with somebody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were two or three uniformed with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you observe what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Listen, I did not really stand for much longer. I guess they were talking about something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you observe how he was dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Camouflage, standard clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see whether or not he had any weapons on his possession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you said you saw him on a second occasion when you were in Omarska. Can you remember approximately or can you remember when that was, the date of that sighting, when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the middle of the following week, about mid-day. We were taken to the dining room for lunch, and going there, on the way there, towards the dining room, I noticed Dule Tadic again roughly at the same place where I had seen him the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, approximately what distance were you from him when you first saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then maybe 10, 15 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you able to get a good view of him on this occasion, on this second occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you remember whether there was anything that interfered with your view, whether it be weather conditions or any other obstruction that prevented you from getting a good view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see whether Tadic was on his own on this occasion or was he accompanied by other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, he was in the company of two or three people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On this occasion can you recall how he was dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same, in camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On both these occasions are you sure that the person you saw there was the accused Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On Friday of that week I was transferred to Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is Friday of the first week of June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent the night, overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We arrived in Trnopolje by bus from Omarska. There were 27 of us. Entering the Trnopolje camp, somebody escorting our bus made a list of our names and said that we would be spending the night there and that tomorrow at 7.00 a bus would come to collect us and take us to Prijedor. We left the bus, entered the camp, Trnopolje. There were friends and colleagues there waiting. I was accommodated in the premises of the library of the school, together with my friend and neighbour, Sulejman Caufe. At 7.00 or 8.00 in the morning when we were told to get ready outside the command building, a man in uniform was there. He swore at us, our God, he said, "Where have you been? We were looking for you last night? The bus has gone." They found 22 people and five of us were missing. I said, "But that was what we were told. What should we do now?" "I do not know, we will see". That was the answer. I went back to the library and maybe only some 15 minutes later Sulejman comes in saying, "Hamdo, they have come to pick us up with a police van". Then I went out together with Suljo and another three men whom I did not know. We entered the van and we were taken to the Prijedor police station. We were then taken to the hall and told to sit down. We sat down. A policeman came and asked, "Who is Hamdija Kahrimanovic?" and I said, "Me" and he told me to follow him. I followed him and he led me through the premises and took me to a room where Simo Drljaca was sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then when you came to Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just outside the room of Simo Drljaca, there was Vokic was standing. I think his name is Radovan. I know he was a student of mine. He was Simo Drljaca's driver and he said the following, "Oh, my teacher. If you had beaten me, I would now pay you back". I just shrugged and entered the room. I sat down. We used to be colleagues at work. He was a lawyer in the centre for elementary education and upbringing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who is "he"? Whom are you referring to as "he used to be a lawyer"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a legal by education in peace time. He was a lawyer in peace time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, but tell us who "he" is. Are you talking about Simo Drljaca, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You asked me what I did outside Simo Drljaca's room. Yes, I am talking about Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened? What did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He offered me a seat. I sat down. I had two glasses of cognac and he said to me, "Look at what your people have done. They went and killed such a good man as Osme". He was Police Commander in Kozarac. Then he listed some other boys, some other men, saying, "You see what your people have done? They have killed them". I just shrugged. I did not know what to say. We sat a while and then he ordered his secretary to write out some kind of certificates with the help of which we could move around. I did not know what address to give him because I did not know where I would be staying, but that was a Saturday and he ordered that I should come back on Monday to tell him my address, and with this certificate we had freedom of movement within the territory of the city of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What period of time did you stay in the city of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed until August 20th 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the period of time that you were in Prijedor city itself, living there, did you ever at any stage see the accused Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him in Prijedor very often, most frequently in the company of Drljaca. I remember a direct contact the two of us had. We ran into each other on the steps of the police station when he said to me, "Hamdo, if we find medicines in your school, you will end up like your secretary, Ante", and I said, "In my school you will find medicines but that will be the first aid kit that every school has to have". Of course, I did not know what had happened to Ante. I later learned that he was in Omarska. You see, I did not know that this kit would be transformed into a large pile of medicines. I was afraid, of course, and I avoided contact with people that knew me. I grew a beard. I put on glasses. I put on a cap on my head when I was doing my work and moving around Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you work while you were in Prijedor, that period of time after you had arrived there from Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, just before the war, about mid-May, I was appointed by the assembly of my school principal of the school, because the previous principal had left and as the end of school year was approaching the school needed a principal, and I was elected. In spite of my refusal because I knew what it meant to be a principal, particularly in view of the times lying ahead, I accepted the will of the absolute majority. After leaving the camp, I was given premises in Prijedor in a kindergarten. I was able to visit Kozarac to see my school, to try to save what could be saved of the property of the school, the pedagogical aids, the financial means. I was driven there by the police with three policemen and my assistant was with me, the secretary, Ante, too. What documentation we could find, we moved to Prijedor and every day I reported for work. The parents would come. Students would come for certificates at the end of the school year. You know what happens at the end of any school year. I continued doing this until August 20th, but it was my assessment that my safety was in jeopardy and it was, indeed, in jeopardy. I was taken twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why did you come to the conclusion that your safety was in jeopardy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military police came twice to pick me up, to take me. I learnt that the military police knew about me or, rather, Miso Radulovic had recommended me to the military police. That is the man I was talking about before, unfortunately -- he was my witness at my marriage, at my wedding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say you saw Tadic several times in Prijedor city when you were there, was he dressed the same way on each occasion that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly the same, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I noticed his camouflage clothes, like military clothes in different colours. I do not know much about uniforms. I know what my uniform was like while I was doing service, probably that was the fashion now. Anyway, he was wearing such a uniform. I saw him very often in Prijedor, as I said, and very often in the company of Drljaca and this Vokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see him about the same area or did you see him in various areas all over Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was doing the work I was doing in Prijedor, my route was always the same, from the kindergarten to the municipality building and the police station, occasionally to the bank building. That was the same path, the same direction, because somehow it had become a habit. I knew the people I was going by. There were lots of checkpoints, lots of patrols, and I had some luck because in my ID papers it said that I was inhabitant of Prijedor. It said Prvomajska 6, Prijedor, and when they saw that I came from Prijedor, it was easy to pass, but people from Kozarac had grave difficulties. Therefore, my route was more or less the same and it was along that path that I saw Dusan Tadic, but most frequently in front of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The police station is sometimes referred to as the SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the same building where the police station was and the other departments of that institution, MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you at any time during 1992 a member of any military, paramilitary, group or any anti-Serb armed resistance group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Just at the beginning of the election activities, I was thinking of continuing in SDP because at that time, I must admit, I was a member of the League of Communists, but in the election campaign I did not join any party and particularly not ethnic parties -- I am a teacher -- because I have children of various ethnic groups whom I teach.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Have you ever met or known of anyone in the Kozarac region or area who looks very much like the accused Dule Tadic and who from time to time has been mistaken for Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you please now look around the courtroom and tell me if you can see the person that you know and recognise as Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is Dule Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you please point to that person and describe for the record where he is located in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is left of me in the middle between two uniformed persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might the record reflect, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The record will reflect that the witness identified Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kahrimanovic, I would like to deal with something, first of all, that you mentioned at the end of your evidence, and that was that you decided not to join any political party during the elections as you felt that, as a teacher, you did not want to be identified with any particular group; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did it seem to you, then, that the people in your area were dividing themselves along ethnic lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what it seemed to me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That the people were identifying themselves with the political party that supported their ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. Muslims SDA, Serbs SDS. There were people belonging to other parties, there were other parties, not just these two ethnic ones, the Reformists, the Liberals, the SDP members etc.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The HDZ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, HDZ. I left it out of course, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In Kozarac, that was a village or town that was principally Muslim, that would have made the SDA a powerful party within that town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In fact, looking at the numbers of different nationalities within Kozarac, the SDA would have been the overwhelming voice of the people who lived within Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the election results, yes, because it was the majority party and the majority people. The Muslims were the majority in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: These elections we are talking about were the ones in 1990; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: After 1990 many people had identified themselves with a political party for the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not quite sure that we can say for the first time, because, you know, from the previous prewar period there was one party, the League of Communists, and certainly that many of the members of that party, the prewar party, accepted and joined new organisations, new parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, you are quite right to refer to the previous political situation before 1990 because there was only one party, but for the first time in 1990 there was more of a choice for the people to identify themselves with other parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: After those elections in 1990, politics and the choices for the people became much more greatly discussed by the citizens than they had in the former days under the Communist government when there was only one political party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The era of democracy, they say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, and this was very much a new era that was to start and for the first time people were experiencing the new politics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You seem to be someone who has lived in this area for many years and know the people. Can you assist me at all as to how Kozarac became principally a place where Muslims lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid I could not tell you how. It would be as if you were to ask me how come that Omarska was a place inhabited exclusively by the Serbs. I suppose it was the will of the people through history through the centuries to decide where they would live. As far as I know, there was no coercion forcing anyone to live here or there. Everybody could live where they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That was going to be my next question, since you had posed it, which was how Omarska, as you described it, became a Serb village or town and why it is identified as such? But it seems you cannot supply me with the answer; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At this time then with the new politics emerging, outside Kozarac were the people aware of the tensions between politicians and the government, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well as the government in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, the general political situation was what it was. Whether there were people who believed that there were differences in the political views between Belgrade and Sarajevo, well, certainly there must have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Presumably, you citizens within Kozarac were aware of these arguments or debates that were taking place at a higher political level beyond you citizens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had occasion to see the Assemblies at the Republic level. We could listen to the Assembly meetings at the communal level, and the same roughly could be said of meetings at the local level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did this cause citizens to identify themselves, perhaps more strongly, with the parties that they favoured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What I am going to suggest to you, you see, is that within Kozarac many of the younger people were identifying themselves very strongly with the SDA, and what it meant to them as young Muslims, perhaps not looking back at history with the experience that older people may have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not my view that those people turned to the young Muslims. This was a process that had swept the whole country. There was infiltration among the youth of the Muslims and their identification with the SDA. The same could be said of the HDZ and the SDS parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes. (11.30 a.m.) (The court adjourned for a short time) (12.05 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you may continue. I apologise for the delay. We had asked someone to indicate to counsel that we were in a plenary meeting discussing matters that required a vote. So I apologise for the delay, but here we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kahrimanovic, I would like to continue asking you some questions about politics in Kozarac. The first thing I want to deal with is this, it is right, is it not, that Kozarac did not have an SDS party founded within it prior to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I ask you something? I have never engaged in politics, and I was not a member of any political party. I was not interested in all that. So, would you please ask me less questions which deal with politics? As for your question, listen, in Kozarac itself one could count on the fingers of one hand the number of people who were members of political parties, and I think that people who lived in Kozarac were active within SDS party which was founded where there were far more Serb inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So, would it be right, if I can take the take end of that answer, that what you are saying is that Kozarac did not have its own SDS party established within that town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if it did or did not. I know that groups of people of Serb ethnic origin often rallied around those people that I mentioned which seems to be indicating that some activity was, indeed, taking place there, and that they were embroiled in the SDS politics because how else can I interpret their meetings, their socializing, their agreements, acceptance and extended arm, a branch of another place, such as Omarska or Prijedor and such like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So what you are saying is that associations between Serb people at this time prior to the conflict you were interpreting as being necessarily connected with politics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just standing back and looking at that, do you not think that is a little bit unfair? You mentioned that Mr. Tadic was with a man called Kesic, you called him Djoko Kesic, do you think it was "Dusan" Kesic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko Kesic -- and Djoko, I did not mention that -- a laboratory technician in the health centre in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We are both talking about the same person you described that seeing him with Dusko Tadic that it was like a tete a tete, as though they were secretly discussing politics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, listen, it was not secret. Had it been secret, it would have happened in some -- in camera somewhere, but they talked as they did. I said that I am not aware that in Kozarac, in this particular locality, there were any particular premises assigned to the SDS, but that their meetings, their associations, their communication, their contacts took place -- were held in places which I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know if Dusko Kesic was ever a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personally, I do not and I also do not know many other people who are members of other parties. I have not seen his application or his membership card. But the very fact that you are usually seen in the same milieu, that you often associate with the same people, allows one to assume that you are a member or a sympathiser, a follower of a particular party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Or Trivo Relic, do you know if he has ever been a member -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Trivo Relic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know if he has ever been a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I saw him in this company, so it applies to him as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But do you know if he has ever been a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to my specific knowledge. I have had no opportunity to learn that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You see, these people that you are saying that Mr. Tadic associated with, you do not know whether they were talking about politics or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But you are assuming as a guess, but I would be right in saying to you that you do not know, and that would be a fair answer to say you did not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I knew they all worked together and co-operated and, surely, they had no other reasons to meet and to talk except for party reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But there would have been a life outside party politics, would there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is all an integral part of politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As you say yourself, you were outside party politics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I did not socialise with people who were members of some of the parties that I knew about, we had nothing to discuss, to talk about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Within Kozarac itself, would it be right to say that certain groups who were in favour of the SDA party had formed checkpoints or guard posts at various buildings and positions in that town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You did not know about the guard post outside the orthodox church quite near to where you lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had heard about various other places, but those other places, they were of different ethnic composition. I also heard another version that the priority task and exclusive task of that guard post was to look after the church, because there were rumours in Kozarac that somebody was about to blow up the church, and the church has not bothered any of Kozarac inhabitants for centuries, so, presumably, they were there to look after the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The orthodox priest that you mentioned, he is Mladen Mejakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, I do not know that individual at all. I have never seen him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you not know him because he lived next door to the church?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I did not know him at all. Probably he only lived there for a very short time because I know that many people changed there in that part. There were a few people. I did not know him. I may have met him that day had we accomplished the mission that we were supposed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You knew that he had fled from Kozarac with his family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was talk about that in the locality, "The orthodox priest is gone, something might happen", and that was why we cared, that we really wanted to bring him back to the locality and have him live with us because we did not think, at least in our view, there were no reasons why he should leave Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He had left with his family, were you made aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That he had left at the beginning of May, in fact, 3rd May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know we were given that mission to try to persuade him to come back somewhere around the middle of May. When he left, I would not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you not know that originally he had left Kozarac and gone to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About his movements and the routes he took were something that I know nothing about at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You did not know anything then about the circumstances as to how he left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But you told us that Mr. Tadic acted destructively because he failed to get the priest to return?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not his mission. His mission was to establish the contact with the priest, so that the priest would receive us and so that myself and Dusko and Kemal Susic could go to him. That contact was not established on two occasions and the third time when we came to him to see if we could go, we did not find Dusko there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you say that contact was not established, did you mean that the priest would not see you or are you saying that Dusko Tadic did not speak to the priest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both alternatives are possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because you told us earlier today that Mr. Tadic had told you that the priest was too busy to see you and did not want to see you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he could not receive us that day because he was too busy and that meant that we would probably be received the next day, and when the next day we returned, and those same people at the same place, the answer was that he was busy again. The third time when Susic and I came, we did not find Dusko at the place we had agreed upon the previous day, and that was it, in front of the coffee bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You expressed that to the court as Dusko Tadic acted destructively, but you did not know what had been said between Dusko Tadic and the priest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is logical; either the priest did not want to receive us or Dusko did not want to establish contact with him. There is no third possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So if the priest did not want to see you, then it would not be right to say that Dusko Tadic had acted destructively?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why did Dusko Tadic not tell us the reason why the priest would not receive us that day? But if the priest was busy today, then he would be free tomorrow. If he was busy tomorrow, then he would see us the day after tomorrow. But I really wonder if it was possible that he could not receive us on any one of those three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, exactly so it would be wrong as you do not know to blame Dusko Tadic if the priest did not want to see you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic had assumed a responsibility of the Civic Council, a member of which he was, and he had to comply with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If he cannot comply with it, that is not his fault, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then he should have told us that the task was beyond him and that we should look for another person through which we could establish the contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, when you told us about the newspaper article and the anonymous letter that had been sent to the Tadic family threatening them, you did not know from your own knowledge who wrote that letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the beginning it was not known, but I said that the ruling party expressed its reservations regarding the letter and its contents, and people were making guesses in Kozarac because never before had anything like that happened. Of course, it was also submitted to the relevant authorities in MUP to conduct the necessary investigation and all the other procedures, that is, decipher the handwriting and so on and so forth. I said that rumour went around Kozarac as to the author of the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exactly. That is what you heard from someone else telling you something about what they had heard from an investigation or, even worse, from many other people speaking to each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Officially, the official interpretation of the police did not exist, and it is quite natural why there was not because it could have caused further conflicts, further problems, and that is perhaps why there was no official communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You say that the SDA party disassociated itself from sending that letter, but that is not to stop anyone having sent that letter unofficially, some young hot heads or older hot heads sending such a letter not officially?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that that news which spread around Kozarac was that the letter had been written by Mira Tadic and that there was such a rumour in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No-one accepted responsibility for sending that letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As far as Kozarac itself was concerned, were not certain people identifying themselves more as proMuslim, proSDA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you unaware of anyone obtaining weapons for themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know. I had no contact. I am telling you. It was of no interest to me, politics and all that. I am telling you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would it have surprised you at the time if you had learnt that is what some people were doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, listen, I would not have been surprised by such an act because in Kozarac I had opportunity to see uniformed people of Serb origin carrying bags with ammunition or a rifle or something. So, if a Serb can carry it around, why not a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So, are you telling us then from what you saw and your own experience and this is how you remember things, that you only saw Serb people in Kozarac carrying ammunition, uniforms, weapons, that you did not see any Muslim people wearing uniforms or carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw Muslims, but they are people that I know were hunters and they had hunting rifles, and why had he -- why did he carry it around on his shoulder or in his hands, I do not really know, but I did not observe anyone carrying that conventional military rifle or some more up-to-date arm, automatic or semi-automatic weapon, and I did see people of Serb ethnic origin. I saw Borovnica carrying an automatic weapon around Kozarac or a fellow called Tepo. His family name could have been Vidovic, I am not sure. Likewise, he would go into a restaurant, armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So, what you are saying is you did not see any people at checkpoints, Muslim people, with any weapons anywhere in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, listen, I did not say that. If -- there were people at checkpoints like that and they said they were members of the Territorial Defence, which was a regular unit attached to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So did you see TO people then before the conflict at various positions in Kozarac with weapons standing guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the guards were of mixed ethnic origin. There were Serbs as well. One of my neighbours, rather, he was not a neighbour, he was the son-in-law of my neighbour, a man called Ljuban -- I cannot remember his surname -- was also one of those guards. They took turns, so it was not a single ethnic guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So, you are saying that it was not just Muslims at guard duty; it was guard duties that involved all people from the community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, members of Territorial Defence because that was the suggestion, that we should control these crossroads to avoid somebody, an unknown person, entering and provoking an incident or something like that. In my assessment, that was the role of those guards at checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the mediation meetings in May in Prijedor, did you attend all those meetings or only some?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I remember attending one meeting. I was invited, but I had my job to do. I was working in the school. I did not go, but all others went and then they would come and inform the citizens what had been agreed with the representatives of the Serb authorities at the time, what is required, what needs to be done, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the one meeting that you attended was that, you say, the one meeting that Dusko Tadic attended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and Zigic Milenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know, in fact, if he attended another meeting but you were not present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: After the attack on Kozarac, you took refuge in a position within the town itself; you did not leave the town like many others did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there in Kozarac on the day of the attack, on Sunday, all the time, all night, the night from Sunday to Monday, and on Monday morning my neighbours had the idea that we should try to seek shelter in the woods. My car was in the yard and we decided that I should go and my next door neighbour, Fazlic Kemal. He took the Saric family in his car and I took the Kusuran family and my brother-in-law, Zijad. We went in the direction of Debeli Brijeg where we had a lovely chalet there. There were lots of people there, horse drawn carriages, tractors, people on foot, limousines. When we had climbed just above the mosque, I left my car -- we saw we could not go any further -- I left my car near a house that was under construction and my neighbour, Kemal, and the Saric family went on. We could not go further because there were shells were falling, so we sought shelter in the cellar of a neighbouring house full of women and children. I spent two or three hours there. Then I saw I could not stay on because it was dangerous, and I told my three friends, "I am going and you think it over". Then they followed me down the so-called Brdjani where late in the afternoon on that Monday we spent a couple of hours and when it was quite dark, we turned back towards our homes, towards the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you would have stayed that night on the Monday night, 25th May, back in Kozarac, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the night between Monday and Tuesday, and the night between Sunday and Monday, I spent the night in Kozarac with the neighbours I have named.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So on 26th May when you joined the column from Mrakovica -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was not a column from Mrakovica; it was a column coming from the direction of Mrakovica. I do not know exactly where they were coming from, but we called it the direction of Rajkovici. This was a column that we joined with the exception of the Fazlic and Saric family whose whereabouts at the time I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I understood what you said and I was quoting from your words this morning. All I wanted to know was at what time you joined that column.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between 7.00 and 8 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tuesday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you got to the bus station on the Banja Luka/Prijedor road, can you tell me what time that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The place where I had joined was about 300 or 400, 500 metres from the Banja Luka Prijedor cross roads. Maybe you need some 10 minutes to reach that junction, but we did not stay there. We went ahead in the direction of Prijedor. We reached the bus station at Kozarusa known as Limenka. There was a big point there, lots of army men, lots of equipment, tanks, guns. This was a checkpoint. We were searched and men were separated from the women and children who went left, we were told to go right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am sorry, my question was, and perhaps you can help me, what time it was that you reached that checkpoint, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe it took us about half an hour to get there from the point at which I joined the column in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said that the people were being separated there, men, women and children, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who was doing that separating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People in uniform, mostly wearing the grey-green uniforms of the former Yugoslav People's Army.
