utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know any of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you got taken to Keraterm where you stayed one night, did you know any of the guards who dealt with you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know any of the guards, but I knew a soldier who entered the camp or rather the room in which we were housed. I even asked him, "Cedo, can you give me a cigarette or two?" This Cedo was my teacher's brother, the brother of Tambic Bozo. He went out and he brought me one or two cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you went to Omarska the next night, did you know any of the guards who had dealings with you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you were taken for interrogation after you arrived, did you know who was questioning you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were five of them. I did not know any one of them personally, though in the neighbouring rooms there were interrogators whom I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just dealing with your own questioning, did you know any of the guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, I did not know anyone. They were not guards. There were five of them in the room in which I was interrogated and I did not know any of them. The police that escorted me, there were three of them. I did not know any of them either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you were put in the place you called the garage, did you know any of the guards who were dealing with you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personally, no, but I would see when the door was open that there was a man in uniform there. But I did not know anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you were taken out on to the pista from the garage, did you know any of the guards there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. They would walk by us, two or three. They were taking turns, but I did not know any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you said about the other people who were interrogating detainees, did you see anyone there that you knew in the interrogation building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are thinking of the other Commission members?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, because you did not know who questioned you or the other people in that room and I am asking whether you knew anyone else in that building whom you saw that you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had occasion at least on that day when we were standing on the pista in the afternoon, they would end their work, they would climb a bus, a small van intended for the miners from Ljubija, and they would leave the interrogation rooms. I saw a colleague of mine, he was a teacher in the 16th May school. His name was Radakovic. I cannot remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was he the only one that you knew getting into that bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only noticed him. I recognised him. I did not know the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said there was an occasion on the pista that you saw Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that Friday, yes, we were allowed to sit down or to get up, to stand there, but where we were on the spot, where we were standing, that is when I saw Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If it is possible, you have got a pointer on the table beside you, are you able to stand up and indicate -- and if the video monitor can now show the model between the interrogation building and the hangar so that we can see on our screens, if we can focus in, please on to the model? I do not seem to have the same control as others! I use that politely.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I can see it. Why do you not try to ask the gentleman to point. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. (To the witness): If you can indicate to us where you were standing at the time you say you saw Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I show this on the model here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I cannot see it on the screen very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do not look at the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The garage is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Keep your pointer there. Yes, we are familiar with the buildings ourselves.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was standing facing the entrance where I entered on Thursday morning. I was halfway along this building, here somewhere I think, so I could see diagonally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, keep your pointer there, please, where you say you were standing just for a moment, where you were standing. Is that where you were standing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sitting and standing at that moment I was standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you could just keep the pointer there where you were sitting and standing when you saw Dusko Tadic? I do not know if there is another shot that the camera men -- yes, they can. That is the one. Perhaps if you could indicate where you say Mr. Tadic was when you saw him on the pista?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly here somewhere, about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. So the point that you indicated was close to the interrogation building, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that where you and the other prisoners were taken from the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You described being on the pista because you and the other detainees were let out and you could stand or sit up. Were you in that area with the other detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please, on that Friday morning when we were allowed out of the garage, probably because it was too crowded inside, they let us stand alongside the building. We asked whether we could sit down, they said we could. Some people were sitting, some were standing and changing positions. Those were the people who had been interrogated on Thursday afternoon. They would then be put in the garage. That is where we had spent the night about 150 or 200 people. Those were the people who had come out and from there in the evening when it became quite dark we were moved in the same direction to one of these garage doors, one or the other, up the stairs to the last room upstairs. We were not joined only by those who had spent the night in the garage, but later on in the afternoon there were other prisoners who joined us. Where they came from, where they had spent the night, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How many of them were there in that group that you describe on the Friday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The evening on Thursday I do not know exactly, maybe 10, 11, 12. When I was brought to the garage after interrogation I was in the second group of five. People were coming, coming, coming and then at one point I counted 150 and I gave up counting. We were so closely packed that no one could sit down. Some of us were standing on one foot. I remember two men, Susic Zijed who fainted, who lost consciousness, there was a small window, there was no air, Denic Junuz, they were thrown out of the door outside to catch some air and then they were brought back in. That was the group on Friday morning that was let out of the garage. They saw that they could not live in that small space. We spent until late in the afternoon there when, as I said, we were moved into that room upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the position you indicated to us by that building was where you were placed with at one stage you counted some 150 other people, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the garage was the place where we were taken after interrogation on Thursday, we spent the night Thursday to Friday. Friday morning we were taken out. We spent the whole day on the pista and in the evening we were moved to that room upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, but perhaps you would like to stand again with the pointer and indicate where you were and I will ask you the question again. Thank you. If we could have the same camera shot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I roughly remember the gate which I entered Wednesday to Thursday, this door. On that Friday I was just opposite that door, maybe a metre left or right, I cannot say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you could just remain standing so that we can see it with the pointer. I want to make sure you understand the question. Can you point to that same place again and leave the pointer there?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He has pointed twice, Mr. Kay. He understands the question. I believe I understand the question and I understand both answers. Why do you want him to point a third time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am just trying to make it clear ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It is perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my mind I think the witness ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are not to determine whether it is clear or not in your mind. We have determined it is clear. You have asked him twice. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will move on. (To the witness): If you could sit down, but ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But you want to say it is still not clear in your mind. It is clear. Move on, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: (To the witness): Were you in that position with some 150 other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the prisoners who had spent the night in the garage, I repeat, on that Friday morning were taken out to the pista. I was among them. We were standing in line one behind the other, a line, we spent the night standing. When we came out on the pista we asked whether we may sit down. We were allowed to sit down, but only one by one lined up. Sitting there you can move left or right. Sometimes you get up a little. That is how we spend the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were there any other prisoners in any other place other than that one you have indicated outside on the pista?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Were there other prisoners from among this group or generally other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Not generally in the camp, but on the pista. You have said that you were with a large group. Were there any other prisoners on the pista ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. So, when you say you saw Mr. Tadic you were actually looking through a large group of people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not say so. Most of the people were sitting down. Occasionally they would get up because they were tired from standing all night, the torture we had experienced during the interrogation, the mistreatment, the harassment. So there was no theoretical chance of anybody obstructing me, obstructing my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The person you looked at you did not look at for a long period of time, only a short moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Long enough to recognise him and I sat down immediately. You know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But it was a short period of time, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite long enough to recognise my neighbour whom I had known for years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because what I suggest to you in fact is that you made a mistake in that short period of time. You did not see Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see you, sir, in Omarska and I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At this stage so far you have not recognised anyone else who has had dealings with you during your confinement in Keraterm, your confinement in Omarska. This is the first person you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Keraterm I said I had met Cedo Tambic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I forget. You are right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People did not communicate with me because there was no need. To tell you the truth, I did not want to communicate because it would be better for me, for them not to see me or to recognise me, because in the Omarska camp there were no orderly records of the names of the persons detained there and precisely to avoid identification, not just me but many others behaved in the same way avoiding contact with others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But you had been a school master in Kozarac for many years, many pupils had passed through the schools where you had taught, and in those three days until the Friday other than the guard who was a son of a colleague of yours, the only person you can recognise is Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next time you say that you saw him was in the middle of the following week about mid-day, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About mid-day, I am not sure whether it was Thursday or Friday. I cannot say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you recollect the date it was that you left Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the Friday of that week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At that stage you had been in the camp three days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I stayed a week before that. I reached Keraterm on 26th. Then on 27th to 28th I was in Omarska. Then the whole week in Omarska and the whole following week in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you recollect how many days it was before you left Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A day or two. It was the middle of that week and I left at the end of the week. Then it must have been a day or two before that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess until 2.30. (1.00 p.m.) (Luncheon Adjournment) (2.30 p.m.) PRIVATE

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Judge Vohrah asked, I think, on the last day for a plan. We have a plan, your Honours. There are three plus an original. I do not know whether your Honours want to mark it as an exhibit? I have given a copy to the Defence. If it is to be marked as an exhibit, it would be 238, but it is a ground floor plan and the first floor plan of the big garage building. The numbers that appear on the plan that is now being handed to your Honours correspond with the numbers as in the model itself.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is it 238, did you say, or do you want to make it an exhibit? 130, I think, is the -----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It could be 130A which, perhaps, might correspond.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will look, I suppose, to 130, but this is really for our ease, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Then 130 is in, but 130A will be admitted as something that it was easier for us to look at when we are not in the court room at least. Very good. There is no objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you. MR. KAHRIMANOVIC, recalled

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just so it is clear, Mr. Kahrimanovic, may I also put to you that, in fact, that second occasion when you say you saw Dusko Tadic that in the circumstances you saw him that you were mistaken, it was not him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you describe what he looked like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Standard uniform, and then slightly, well, not really a beard but a growth, not particularly well kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Witness, I do not understand at all this evidence that you gave about medicines at the school. What was the importance of there being or not being medicines found at the school? Can you explain that to me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. By Statute, every school was to have a first aid kit, either in a box or a bag, and the kit included bandages, plastic small scissors, a needle or something, in case a pupil would be injured outside the building or around the school building, in the school yard, so that first aid could be extended to him or her. It was important because my secretary, that is, the school secretary, he was Ante Zlotaj, the school secretary, found himself in the camp at Omarska again because one of the members of those SDS troops, I do not know whom, when going through the school found a contingent of such medicines and they thought there were medicines, some medical supplies, prepared for combat operations possibly. So in my school there was such a first aid bag which included this and it was to serve the purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you very much, that explains it. The second question I wanted to ask you was when you say that you saw the accused in Omarska twice, is your recollection that the person you saw was bearded or without a beard on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as for the beard, no, he was simply unshaven. That is what I mean. That is what he looked like. I mean, when a beard, then it is already a growth of hair; whereas he looked as if unshaven.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. The last question I wanted to ask you relates to the priest who had left the town and your task initially was to try to secure his return. That being so, did you not make some enquiry as to why he had left and what were you told as to why he had left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not enquire about that. Personally, I think he left it for reasons of security. I believe he knew what awaited our town and that was why he left because we felt, we thought that there was no reason for it, that we had lived there together until then, and we also wanted perhaps to recover our self-confidence by bringing him back into our environment because there was no reason why. But he did leave, so evidently he had some reason to do so and, presumably, that meant that he knew something that we did not know.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: But no-one gave you any explanation for his leaving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I would know about.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not since he left.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kahrimanovic, you testified that 27 persons left on a bus to the Trnopolje camp, is that correct? Then when you left there were 22 of you. My question is what happened to the other five, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try to explain. There was a misunderstanding. From Omarska we were taken by a bus and there were 27 of us. We arrived in front of the Trnopolje camp and then we were all filed by person who escorted us, that is, we were put on record and we were told to manage for ourselves and to spend that night there and then the next day a bus would come to the command building, and then take us from there to Prijedor. So, it depended on how people managed; I managed somehow because I had some friends and colleagues there and I was taken there, that is, they took me to the school library. That is where I spent the night. In the morning I went to the command building as it had been agreed to report there or enquire about a superior. I do not know what had happened to the bus that we had been told the previous evening would come to take us to Prijedor. He cursed my God and used other four letter words and said, "Well, where are you? We were looking for you all night and we managed to find 22 of you and to put on the bus and take them to Prijedor", and then I asked him, "And what about us? What do we do?" "Whatever you can manage", and meanwhile the camp commander arrived, Slobodan Kuruzovic, who was a school fellow of mine, and I asked him, "Slobo, you know that we arrived last night, and this night this happened they had found 22. I know no reason for which they should take those 22 and what are we supposed to do now?" He said, "I do not know, wait". So I went back to the school library and a few minutes later my colleague, Sulejman Causevic, came, and said, "They are asking for you, Hamda". So I and another three persons came out, I do not know who they are, but that is those last five, and we were put in a police car and taken to SUP office. So the next day we were all there, all 27 of us.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I have another question. It is a general question, sir. You have lived in Kozarac or did live in Kozarac your whole life, I gather, is that correct, until recently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, I said I was born in Kozarac and that is where I came out from the latter part of the primary school, that is the last four years, I passed examinations to come out of the primary school and I lived in Kozarusa with my parents when I return from my military service until 67, 68 when I finished, and then in 68 I built my own house. Until then I lived in my family house and in this house, of course, I lived until 26th May '92.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I gather that you have taught both Muslims and Serbs in the school where you were a school teacher and then a principal, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. While I was the principal, I did not teach because I was the principal. So I had to perform the duties of the principal, but before I was assigned deputy principal in '74, I worked in classrooms, and after '74, after my second term as a principal, I went back to teaching but then to the school in Kozarusa which had been built meanwhile as the primary school eight grade elementary school, but as a part of the school in Kozarac until '82 when I was again appointed a principal of that school. While I was in Kozarusa, I was the, how shall I put it, as a host. I was a supervisor there, that is, I did not rank the same as the principal of the school in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: My question really related to your having taught Muslim and Serb children; I gather Serb children go to school with Muslim school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You testified that you have persons of other religion in your family. You lived in a neighbourhood where there were Serbs, is that correct? Is all of this correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My next door neighbour was a Serb, a very good man.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So I guess my question ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He died in my wife's hands.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: -- is perhaps not a fair question, I do not know that you could give a complete answer, but perhaps you can help me to understand since I am not from that area. How could you explain that some of the atrocities that we have heard have been committed, generally I am talking about, throughout the former Yugoslavia, how can you explain that something like that would happen? Given your background, given your experience, knowing that Serbs and Muslims lived together, went to school together, intermarried, how did it happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult to answer, this question. I am also at a loss. I have the keys to my next door neighbour who was a Serb, but he had my keys. That is how we looked after each other, one another. We visited each other for holidays. My best man at my wedding was a Serb. We were friends and he was the same one who threatened us. It is inexplicable what happened to those people. It was some kind of madness. I mean, one did not know whom to trust any more and I do not have a word of explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to this witness being permanently -- any additional questions, Mr. Niemann, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Mr. Kahrimanovic being permanently excused? Very good. You are permanently excused, Mr. Kahrimanovic. Thank you very much for coming. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, could you call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I call Zijad Jakupovic. ZIJAD JAKUPOVIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you take that oath, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You may be seated, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is your name Zijad Jakupovic and were you born on 8th September 1956?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were you born, Mr. Jakupovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Kozarac, Hrnici 107, the village of Hrnici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How far is the village of Hrnici from the centre of the town of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A kilometre-and-a-half.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you attend your primary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you attend secondary school in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When at secondary school did you do a course in building construction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was a course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you live at your property in Hrnici up until 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you initially employed as a bricklayer and then subsequently did you work land in an agricultural sense in the Hrnici area after you had done this, after you had worked as a bricklayer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you in the army from July 1975 to 1976?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you do your military service in an artillery unit and did you attend your military service in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you by nationality and religion a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know the accused Dule Tadic in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember when you first met him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time we were in primary school in Kozarac together, that is in the 6th, 7th and 8th grades we were together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you in the same class as Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Although you lived in the village of Hrnici which is close to Kozarac, did you see him from time to time in Kozarac throughout the course of your life up until 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him often.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us very briefly where he lived in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kozarac, he lived -- he has a restaurant and above this restaurant is next to Perusa -- Perusa was his next door neighbour, that is his nickname, Perusa and Hankic was the surname -- that is, there is this coffee bar and above it is his house. There, I think, is a shop and I believe there is yet another home, I cannot remember their name, the name of the man between the shop and Dule's coffee bar, is yet another house and beyond his house is the road leading to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So far as you know, did he live, he and his family, at this place all the time that you knew him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, they had lived there all their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what Dule Tadic did in Kozarac for a living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he coached karate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After he coached karate do you know what he did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, after that he had the coffee bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know his father's name -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: If this is merely for the purpose of qualifying him as somebody to identify, surely that has been sufficiently done?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours feels so, that is fine. (To the witness): Do you recall when Kozarac was attacked in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It was on 24th May 1992 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you at home at the time when the attack occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you do immediately the attack started, where did you and your family go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I went back home to the cellar and we hid there with my wife and children and other members of the family while the shelling lasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then receive instructions over the radio for people to report to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the radio they were informing us and I learnt that in Trnopolje a kind of a reception centre was being formed, that we were all to report there, so that I took my family and went out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Trnopolje, some six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you then transferred to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went to Keraterm were you placed in a large room with about 200 other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: While you were in Keraterm were you beaten or mistreated in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was, that is, beaten by Duca and Zigic -- not once, many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "Duca", to whom are you referring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am referring, I did not know Duca before the war. I met him in the Keraterm camp. "Duca" is his nickname. I believe he is called Dusan Knezevic. "Dusan" is his first name. I am not sure about "Knezevic".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On how many occasions were you beaten by Dusan or Duca Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he sometimes would come in the morning, sometimes in the evening, and some meanwhile by car in civilian clothes, and he would do what he had come to do, that is, beat us and be on his way again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the appearance of Duca Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You have just said a moment ago in your evidence that you knew Dusan Tadic or Dule Tadic. In your mind, is it possible to confuse the two men by looking at them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is there any particular reason why you say the two men are not similar to each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as they were more or less of the same height, except that Duca was very well built, very broad shoulders. He had a round face, and he looked younger.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed between 15 and 16 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went to Omarska where did they place you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They put us in the white house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: While you were in the white house at Omarska, did you ever see the accused Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell me approximately when this was that you saw him -- in Omarska camp, I mean, the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly the date, it was about 21st June, 21st or 22nd. I do not remember exactly, but around that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell me approximately what time of the day it was when you saw him, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately, to tell you truth, I did not have a watch because they took our watches away but it was the afternoon. I think it was about 3.00 or 4.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were you precisely when you first saw Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the white house, entering the white house, the right-hand room.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You were near the entrance to the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Me? Would you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you sitting near the entrance to the white house, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was sitting inside, in the room in the white house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. The answer that I have here in the transcript to the question is, "I was in the white house, entering the white house, the right-hand room". You were already in the white house, I take it, you did not enter it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was sitting in the white house and I was looking through the window when I saw Dusko Tadic. It is the room, the first room, to the right. That is what I said. I spent 15 days there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How for away was Dule Tadic from you when you first saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly, he was not far away from the window, seven to 10 metres away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you recognise him when you first saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you able to see all of him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How much of him could you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just saw the upper part of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that from the waist up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, from the waist up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from being obstructed in seeing that part of him, were you obstructed from seeing any other part of him as he came past that window?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was sitting below the window sill, in front of me was the window sill so I could not see the lower part of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But apart from that did you have a clear view of him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were the weather conditions fine on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you able to keep him under observation for some time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not long -- just as he passed by beneath the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was he walking or standing still when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Walking.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was he with anybody or was he on his own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two other guards with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Had you seen him with these people before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any particular reason or any particular factor that triggered your recollection of Tadic when you saw him on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only reason was that I already had some experience with camps, if somebody recognises you, because mostly acquaintances killed their own, their acquaintances, their colleagues from work, and I was afraid. I was afraid he might recognise me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So it was because you knew him that made you more attentive when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall how he was dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember he had the top part of a camouflage uniform, no cap on his head and a shirt, camouflage shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you able to see whether or not he was armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I could not see whether he was carrying anything in his hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you able to see where he appeared to be going?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was moving towards the entrance of the white house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you actually see him enter the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I could not see him enter. I just heard that somebody entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say you "heard", did you hear footsteps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, like footsteps, you could hear somebody walking.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The footsteps that you heard were consistent with him and two other guards entering the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whose footsteps they were. I just heard footsteps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long were you in the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the white house, 15 days roughly. I do not know exactly whether it is was 15 or 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Had you seen Dule Tadic in the white house on any other occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I saw him just that once.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever see him again in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see him leave the Omarska camp on that day that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the period 1992, were you a member of any military, paramilitary group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you please look around the courtroom and tell me whether you see the person that you know as Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is he sitting between the two policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I think he has described it, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The record will reflect that the witness described the accused -- identified the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jakupovic, you mentioned that it was about 21st or 22nd June that you say that you saw Dusko Tadic in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you tell me how you are able to specify either of those days, 21st or 22nd June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could specify those days because from the day I went to the camp, and the time I spent in Trnopolje and Keraterm, plus the white house and then after I came to the white house, three or four days later I met -- I saw Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. What I am asking about is how you are able to pick out either of those two dates of 21st or 22nd June.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not pick out those two dates. I do not remember whether it was 21st or 22nd. I said 21st or 22nd, roughly. I do not remember the date. I came from Keraterm, how should I say, I was beaten up. I was fighting for my life. I did not know what date it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So it could have been a date other than 21st or 22nd June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could not be any other date because I know. That is why I said "roughly" because I know how many days I spent in Trnopolje, how many in Keraterm, how many in the white house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On that occasion that you said you saw him, you had been in the white house how many days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was four or five days in the white house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said that you were sitting in the room on the right-hand side; was that sitting on the floor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes -- no, not on the floor. We had, like, a small bench which was on the floor but it was not very high.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How many other people were in the room with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that room there were another 10, about 10 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were they like you, sitting down or any of them standing up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, some were sitting. The bench was small. Only two or three people could sit on the bench. Most of them were sitting on the floor, on the concrete, most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were looking out of the window and you would be looking to the area of the pista in between the interrogation centre and the hangar building at Omarska, would that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was looking straight through the window and you cannot see the pista through the window because the pista is a little to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So if you looked out of that window, what view would you have of the camp from where you were sitting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From where I was sitting, I could just see straight ahead the other building, straight ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: From the position that you were sitting in, you could not see the grass in front of the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Grass? No, how could I see the grass in front of the white house when I was sitting low down and the sill was just below the window? So I just saw a little bit in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you say you saw Dusko Tadic, do you know where he was walking from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was coming from the direction of the pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: From the position where you were sitting, can you see the path up to the door of the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, you cannot see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: From the position you were sitting then what you saw of that man, are you able to describe what he looked like? What was his appearance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the upper part of his body, as I said, was in a camouflage uniform like a shirt without a cap on his head. He had a small beard, actually an unshaven, not a big beard, not an old beard, not a big beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The position that you were looking at him from, presumably, you only saw him very briefly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but enough to recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In those circumstances, you were sitting down on that bench in the room that you have described and can you remember what you were doing before you say you saw this man, what was happening in the room where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember nothing was happening in the room. When somebody was coming, and they usually came to the white house for beating, that was regular, and then everybody would fall still, waiting for somebody to come to our door.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was the door to your room open or shut?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shut.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You have described two other men whilst you were at Keraterm, one of them called Zoran Zigic and the other one Dusan Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said that you had dealings with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes -- no, I had no contact. They beat me. They beat me to death.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know anyone else in Keraterm, any of your other guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who else did you know in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just knew somebody called Kailj, Kajin, something like that, and I did not know any other guards. I did not know this one either before, but he was in charge of one of the shifts, so I do not really know whether that is his name or nickname. I just remember the name "Kajin".

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In Omarska did you know anyone else who was a guard there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew Pirman, but I met him in the camp too. Among the guards in Omarska, those that I knew from before was Janjic Nenad, known as "Neso".

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Any others that you knew from before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No-one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you could describe for us so that it is clear, in the room that you were sitting in whereabouts the bench was that you were sitting upon. If you opened the door, whereabouts was the bench?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was next to the wall. The bench was leaning on the wall, opposite the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have nothing in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Witness, when you say you saw the accused out of the window, he was with two other men, were they one behind the other or were they walking abreast of one another?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were going one beside the other.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: If the three were abreast of one another, beside one another, where was Tadic in that group of three, according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tadic was the first next to the white house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have no questions. Mr. Jakupovic, is there any objection to Mr. Jakupovic being permanently excused? Mr. Jakupovic, you are permanently excused. Thank you for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger will be taking the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, if I told you that was a record 20 minutes, what would you say, instead of two to three hours! OK. Mr. Tieger, would you call your next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Before I call the next witness, I wanted to alert the court to a potential problem. The witness has a severe hearing problem which he has had since he was a child. We made an effort the other day to check to see if the equipment here would enable him to communicate with the court. At one point we found that it was nearly impossible and then with some adjustments it seemed that the communication was even better than is normally the case for the witness. So I trust that may be the case at this point, but I wanted to let the court know that we might be dealing with this kind of a problem. In addition, I wanted to alert the interpreters. I will attempt to speak slowly, so that they can follow my questions sufficiently slowly to make communication as effective as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I suppose there is no way to increase the audio, whatever, in the earphones? If you do that, do you do it for everyone? I know that, but there is a maximum. Have you checked to see whether anything can be done? We, of course, press the volume up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Apparently, if the volume is too high it interferes with his hearing aid. There is an appropriate level and I guess he will have to find it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will be flexible. I am sure that if we are patient we will be able to find that level. OK. Call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. The Prosecution calls Dzemal Deomic. DZEMAL DEOMIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you take that oath, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Sir, your name is Dzemal Deomic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What year were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: March 20th 1959. I was born in Kamicani.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How far is Kamicani from the centre of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Are you a Muslim by nationality and religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am by religion a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Deomic, what was your occupation before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was engaged in construction work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know the accused in this case, Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For how long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From our school days, in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you see him many times in Kozarac as you were growing up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After you grew up did you continue to see Dusko Tadic in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. After you grew up did you continue to see Dusko Tadic in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him for the last time in his cafe Nipon before the war, three weeks before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you see Dusko Tadic in Kozarac at other places besides his cafe Nipon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would see him everywhere, at the disco club, he was a member of the fire brigade, and in many other places, in restaurants, in open air gardens, everywhere I saw him. I would sit with him in Kozarac on the terrace. We would talk about his work. He was working in the cafe. I did not have a job. I could not work for him because I had some work scheduled in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Are you referring to a discussion you had with him about the possibility of working at his cafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was a good worker and a relative of mine worked for him and I would help my relative to cover the building as soon as possible to build the roof and then I went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was the roof at Dusko Tadic's cafe or house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His cafe was next to the asphalt road and the old house was behind the cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Deomic, were you in Kamicani when Kozarac was attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you at home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you leave your house after the shelling began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was sleeping at home. The shelling woke me up. I got up, went out in front of the house, and in Kamicani in the streets, in the roads, one could see all on fire, burning, everything collapsing from those shells, buildings falling down, and my house was not hit by a shell until I went down -- I was trying to look for my people to see where they had gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you wounded after you left your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was wounded. As I was moving from my house to the sawmill some 700 metres, I was hit in front of the house of Hrustic, and there were his two sons, one of his sons lost two hands and I was hit and injured in the lower back and I still have some metal of that shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you then go to a shelter where members of your family were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That night did you stay there or did you go to the forest to seek shelter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was that the forest area near Brdjani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you stay in the forest for two nights, that first night and the next night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the shelter in the evening, we moved towards Softici, then towards the village of Brdjani, and we dropped in a house before we entered the forest, and then a neighbour of mine went to look for some doctors who would know how to do things. She had a gas lamp to see where the wound was and if she could help, but it was not possible to help it because the metal had got stuck in the bone, and then towards the midnight we climbed down the hill in the forest to Brdjani.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On the third day of the attack did the people of Kozarac begin to surrender?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those attacks, as far as I remember, on the second day, I mean, our folk had to move towards Kozara and on every house, on every building, on every mosque, there were flags showing surrender, but we did not want to surrender and we went on towards Kozara.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You decided not to surrender with those people who were going towards Kozarac with white flags?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some families, those, for instance, who had women and children and who did not want to escape to flee towards the Croatian borders, some of them surrendered and moved towards Trnopolje, and most of us who did not surrender, we were fleeing towards Kozara.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So, you were heading up toward the mountain, into the mountain area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you captured by Serbian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At that point were you alone or with a group of other people who were trying to flee over Kozara mountain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were trying, half of the people escaped -- they did not want to surrender and some of them fled, we do not know what happened to them -- and half of them surrendered. Down there there was a stream. We were up on the hill on Kozara mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where were you taken after you were captured by the Serbian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They captured us in the woods. On the top there was a soldier. He had some insignia ranks and he had a megaphone, and he told us over the megaphone to surrender, that the Red Cross would help us and there was nothing to be afraid of, and we believed that story and after that, all sorts of things .....

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you and the others who were captured with you taken to a place called Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the group which we surrendered, we had our hands up, and were coming down in the column to the river, and up on the slope next to me we saw a body, a soldier had been killed. Then there is another hillock and there is a clearing -- no, there is a clearing and there is crushed stone there, and we then lied down three by three as we were moving, and then they order us to take out everything we had in our pockets, to empty our pockets, that nothing was to be left in our pockets. We had to empty our pockets and put it above our heads and put our hands behind our head and nose to the sand. Then they started collecting with bags, with the stick going through the things that we had. Next to me was Salid Hrustic. He had a Croatian dinar and the Serb got him by the scruff of his neck, took him some 20 metres away and he was lying on his back, and he fired at him from his hunting rifle from the face and from the back. After that we had to wait for another two or three hours and vehicles, trucks, came to fetch us. We were loaded on to those trucks and then we were taken to Uspine at Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just one question about that, Mr. Deomic: was your friend Mr. Hrustic shot and killed because they found Croatian dinars on him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you arrived at Benkovac were there Serbian troops there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was done with you and the others who had been brought to Benkovac once you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We came to -- we came up to the stage, the stage which was there for various events, for various performances. We came up to that. We had our hands at the back of our heads. I do not know how many of us because we were too many. Then they started questioning them one by one; first, Meho Alic's son from Kamicani. He was taken to the shed and he was beaten. He was so beaten that he could not bear the pain, so he screamed and they killed him straightaway. Then Senad and Hamid and all the others were coming after him. Softic's father was severely battered, but he endured. He did not let out a sound and he was returned to us. So, a number of them were taken to the sheds and nobody came out, not more than one-third of us remained. Two or three hours passed by and we went to have our names put on record and where we were from, and then we were taken into the sheds. There were showers there from some former campaign or something, and that is we spent, we had very eventful nights there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to have marked for identification as Prosecution 238, 238A and B, the following two photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I ask for a favour, please? It is too loud and I also hear some other interference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly we will take care of that immediately. Thank you for telling us. Is that better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you please say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is that better? OK. Mr. Deomic, do you recognise what is shown in these two photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Does one of the photographs show the stage at Benkovac which you spoke about and ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- does the other photograph show the sheds you referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, those can be called up on the screen as soon as I find out which is A and which is B. If we could call up 53/9, that is 238A?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we are attempting to locate Benkovac and as much as we encourage you sometimes to move along, can you help us, perhaps, on one of the maps? Can we locate it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you will give me just a moment, I will check with Miss Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Maybe the witness can tell the general area, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Deomic, can you tell the court approximately where Benkovac is located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Benkovac is located not far from Mrakovica, some four or five kilometres away. As you head for Mrakovica from Kozarac, there is a junction there you move where there was a summer work campaign organised, that is, as you moved towards Mrakovica from Kozarac, from the junction you turn off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So if one followed the road from Kozarac toward the top of Mrakovica, toward the top of the mountain, you would get to the junction to Benkovac first before you reached Mrakovica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before, yes, before -- before to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we call up 53/9, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Does this show the sheds or barracks at Benkovac which you referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we now call up 53/12? Mr. Deomic, does this show the stage where prisoners were lined up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not believe I have tendered 238A and B yet and I would do so now.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Which is the stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The stage is B, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to 238A and B?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. 238A and B will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Deomic, how long were you held at Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three days and two nights.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then were you ordered on to buses and taken to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us how prisoners were made to board the buses in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were driving us, I do not know what the reason was, but all of us, all of us, who had to board buses had to show three fingers and run towards the buses. I could not hear that well, so I was walking, I had my arms outstretched and the Serb got me by the scruff of my neck, took me back and they put me against a wall and hit me on my hand with the butt of his rifle. Then he showed three fingers to me. Then I had to show three fingers on both my hands and to crawlingly approach the bus, and there were military lined up every two or three metres and they were all beating me until I reached the bus. Then they pushed at us, pushed us on to those buses, and in a couple of minutes they closed the door. There were a couple of soldiers in the bus and we started off slowly, very slowly, towards Kozarac. Before we started off, we had to sing their song, their anthem, "Who says who lies". So we started towards Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The song "Who says who lies", is that a Serbian nationalist song?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I wonder if you could ask the witness to sit back a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Deomic, if you could just sit back a little bit? That will be fine. When you arrived in Omarska where were you first held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They put us in the first shed to the right on the corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Using the pointer which is on the table in front of you, just to your right, can you point to the place where you were first held when you came to Omarska. You can stand up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (The witness indicated on the model). Here on the corner, here. The first garage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You may be seated. That is a small garage in the building where the kitchen is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The kitchen is behind it at the end on the corner and next to my garage was another, well, something like a garage but it was not a garage. It was a big room with two pillars and very many people were put in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Deomic, I would like to show you a couple of pictures. May I have these two photographs marked as 239A and B, your Honour? Mr. Deomic, can you recognise what is shown in those two photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, 100 per cent, it is 100 per cent that that is where I lived the first day I was brought from Benkovac in that first garage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do those photographs show the garage from the outside and from the inside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender 239A and B.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 239A and B will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May we first call up 25/10, that is, Exhibit 239A? Mr. Deomic, does this show the garage, the small garage, in which you were held looking at it from the outside? If you look at the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. I guess I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is that the same picture on the television screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Deomic, I am referring to the television screen directly in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Does that show the outside of the garage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we now show 25/19, Exhibit 239B? Mr. Deomic, does this now show the inside of the garage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How crowded was this garage with prisoners when you were placed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was crammed. It was overcrowded with people. At the entrance by the door into that garage, there was about one metre square free, but further inside there was no room for an egg to fall between two persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were the doors to the garage sometimes kept closed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there difficulty for the prisoners to get enough air?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were prisoners provided with enough water while they were in the garage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was very difficult to get water. It was very difficult to get water. Then we asked, then we said that we would break a few windows so as to get some air because with the door closed it was terrible. It was hot, no oxygen, and we moved in a column by the windows, the windows which we broke to get some air, and so we circulated and circulated, on and on. Then some of us asked the guards to bring us some water but they did not want to. They ordered us that we would get more water if we would sing. Then we had to sing their song again, and they did not like it. We had to do it louder, so we would start to sing a little bit louder, and then it was no good either, and then even more louder, and then we would start singing more louder, they would pass some water through the window, or sometimes they would throw it at us so that all the water was spilt. Sometimes one would get it on the face or we were given a can of water.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was that water fresh water or was there something wrong with it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The water was -- one had to drink it because one had to, but it was, but it was stale. It was polluted. There was something in it, as if it has gone through the sewers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were prisoners taken from the garage and beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: While you were in the garage were you taken out of the garage for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you beaten during your interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was another prison called into your room while you were being interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you asked whether or not that prisoner had a gun before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: OK. Was the prisoner, the other prisoner, asked whether or not you had a gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you both answer "no" or that you did not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They beat us and beat, and I was down on my knees, and my hands were down on my legs and head bowed down. I had to wait what would happen, and then I had to repeat again whether I knew where he had hid it, to tell them and then they would stop beating us. I was telling them, "I do not know. You can kill me but I do not know. I do not know". And then a solder would come from the back with a pistol and he put it into my mouth and with his finger on the trigger and he asked me, "Where is it? Tell us where it is". But, evidently, the gun was empty and it did not fire even though he pulled the trigger, and another -- the other one covered him with something, with something like a small rug and covered his head, and said that he would kill him unless we admitted where the rifles were, but we were saying we did not know. Nobody was killed at the interrogation with me, only we got quite a lot of beatings on our legs, back, on the head, and all over.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes. (4.00 p.m.) (The court adjourned for a short time) (4.20 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Mr. Deomic, for approximately how long were you held in the garage, the small garage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately four weeks, three weeks before the interrogation and then after interrogation I was in a very poor condition because of the beatings and I had great problem with my stomach. I had bloody diarrhoea for seven days and nights. I ate nothing, nor could I.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: While you were in the garage, did you see Dusko Tadic in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we call up 239B on the screen, please? Actually, if I may, could I have the original placed on the elmo, if we are going to have the witness use it for indication purposes? Mr. Deomic, were you inside the garage when you saw Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Using the pointer can you use the photograph to your right rather than the screen but use the actual photograph which is to your right ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- to point our where you were? Mr. Deomic, you will need to use that, if you can look to your right first, not to the right on the screen. Miss Sutherland, can you point Mr. Deomic to that? Thank you. Can you show us on that photograph approximately where you were when you saw Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was roughly here, 1 metre 20 centimetres from the door and less than a metre from the wall, roughly here, there. This semicircle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was the door open on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were there any prisoners blocking your view of the outside?
