utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the front. There were prisoners behind me. Sometimes they would push a little to relax. It was not possible to move. There was perhaps 1 metre 30 centimetres space left and right. The door was open to the left, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where was Dusko Tadic when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic was outside the garage, maybe eight to 10 metres. Next to the van there was a soldier, a guard, standing here. They stopped and talked a little. Then all the others started moving away as much as possible and he was there next to the van with a soldier about eight to 10 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you see from what direction he had come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you show us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came from the direction of Omarska, from Omarska to the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: OK. On the picture, that is from left to right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the left of me, he was coming from my left side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you do anything when you saw Dusko Tadic standing outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I saw him coming with this young boy, a young soldier, a Serb, I was afraid that he might see us, so I pushed backwards to get as far away as I could inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you able to back behind other prisoners so you could not be seen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand. Could you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you able to move behind other prisoners in an effort not to be seen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there near the door. We were afraid -- there was air from the outside so I got somewhere midway, halfway.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall what Dusko Tadic was wearing on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that he had come on a motor bike. He had a band on his head. He was a little unshaven. He had a beard, a small beard, and he had a jacket full of pockets rather like pilot's jacket and trousers, I think black, I am not 100 per cent sure, but I recognised him. On his back he had an automatic rifle with a double chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After the period of time when you were held in the garage, where in camp were you moved to? Where were you then held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that we were transferred to the white house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During the time you were in the white house were you interrogated for a second time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you beaten during that second interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How severely or how badly were you beaten during the second interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They beat me with all kinds of things, with a metal rod, with wires, with soldiers' boots. He kicked me in the area of the kidneys. I had to draw how I had escaped and how I had got there. Then they wanted to know where I had hidden my gun and I said I did not know, most of us fled this way. I said I did not know, and they beat me and beat me, and then there was old judge, a policeman, from Banja Luka. He begged me to admit so that I could be returned home. I said I did not know, I did not know, kill me rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In what part of the white house were you held, in which room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The corridor, along the corridor, the second room to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were there other prisoners in that room with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my room there were just 158 people. In another room it was not so full as it was in my room. Everyone had a bit of space.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you say 158, how do you know that number so precisely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had to count, so as to know which one of us would go either for exchange or for interrogation. You never knew when they would come for you. Mostly there were five or six of us. We repeated. One would count and then another one would repeat, everything is OK, 158 men. For a couple of nights, five or six people would be missing, nobody knew why, and then at night they would come in a drunken state, whoever was crouched, sleeping and if he touched you, you had to get up without whispering or talking and go out quietly and we never knew where they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did some prisoners return after groups were taken out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did any of the rare prisoners who returned explain what had happened to the others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry. I did not understand that. Can you repeat, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When it happened that someone returned after being called out with a group, did you learn from that person what had happened to the others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All kinds of things happened. At the other end, at the entrance to the white house in a room to the left, there were many beaten up men. They were intellectuals, teachers, doctors, journalists, all kinds of people were there, and they had a hard time. Some of them were beaten to death. It was hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was the condition of prisoners in your room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conditions were very, very poor. Some nights, five or six Serbs would come in bearing a Muslim flag, put it in the middle of the room, so that each one of us inmates had to spit at our Muslim flag, and to swear that we would never be Muslims, that we would be Serbs and all kinds of things. Then they would beat us on the head. You would never know what would happen at night. We could not sleep. You could not feel normally. He hit me with a knife. He asked me where my gun was. I said, "I do not know". Then he would kick me in the chin. It was terrible. Every night, five or six times they would come and beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were prisoners in your room forced to beat each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rarely did inmates who were taken out for interrogation for a month, 10, 12 days, then they would come back in the day time after interrogation, and in the evenings when they did not come back from interrogation, then some soldiers would barge in who were guards in the camp, they were drunk, and you do not know what could happen. They would suddenly barge in and hit us on the head, and a relative of mine, Ramasan Sovada(?), he was fat. They put him in the middle, two or three soldiers on each side beating him with all kinds of things until he lost consciousness, and then he cried out. You just could not bear it and you could not be at peace to sleep. It was horrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you remain in the white house until the time came for your transfer to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you and other prisoners ordered to clean the white house before you were transferred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I cleaned it and another two, one from Kozarusa and another one from Prijedor, we had to clean it up. The guard would order us where to go. There was a small room at the end of the corridor, some kind of a canteen. Then we had to go to the hangar. It was flooded. The toilet, the sewage was blocked, and it was filthy. All the filth was floating. We had to take water from the tap and go outside the white house and clean each of the rooms. At the approach to the white house, the first room to the left was a small room. It was full of blood and one did not know how to remove the blood from the walls and the floor. When we had done that, then we said we had finished. We sat on the grass behind the white house, and they read out the groups A, B, C, D, where they were going. We did not know where we would be going. They said some would be going for exchange, some to Trnopolje, some home. Then our group from the white house, we were in the yard, we were transferred to the hangar. Upstairs to the right there was a large room and we waited there. Afterwards, they came for us and then we were lined up in the hangar and they lined us up, those for Trnopolje, those for exchange, but nobody mentioned Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By the time you were transferred, how many prisoners were left in your room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were only eight prisoners in my room left and 150 disappeared. If only the world -- I do not know what happened, if it had not happened on time, who knows when my turn would have come.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During the time you were in the white house, did you see Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw Dusko Tadic twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where were you when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the corner next to the wall at the entrance to the next room. I was crouching in the corner. Dusko Tadic was in the corridor. The door was closed. I saw him twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You say the door was closed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is it possible to see through a portion of that door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have this photograph marked as Exhibit 240, I believe?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Will the roof come off the white house?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, and the camera is also set up for it. Mr. Deomic, do you recognise what is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognise to the right my room where I was while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender this photograph as Exhibit 240 and ask that 22/22 be called on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to 240?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 240 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Deomic, does the photograph now on the screen show the door to your room in the white house, the second room on the right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is a portion of that door at the bottom solid and a bigger portion on the upper part made of glass?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The door was glassed in. I was here, next to the corner, to the right, when you enter to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Deomic, I am going to ask you -- first of all, I will ask the technician if he can assist us with the camera -- in just a moment to stand up and point out some places in the white house. You will not be able to speak to us when you do so, but if you could take that pointer with you?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, there was at least last week we had an extension cord on this microphone. I think he can stand here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Deomic, if you want to respond to any question, you will be able to speak in the microphone to your left which is on the table next to you. So first, sir, can you point out where your room was?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you show us where you were when you saw Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The corner here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you show us where Dusko Tadic was when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You can take your seat. Mr. Deomic, are you able to recall all the details of the times, the two times, when you saw Dusko Tadic in the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to say whether I am ever sure 100 per cent that I know something, but I am certain 100 per cent that I saw him twice. He came to the corridor. There was a soldier with him. I do not know that one. He looked into the room A4. He cast a glance. He looked around and then he slowly turned around towards our room. I crouched down and hid myself so he would not see me. I do not know what he was looking for, why he had come, but I cannot remember 100 per cent the details. But I am sure that I saw him, that it was he.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You have kept a recollection of seeing Dusko Tadic in the white house to this day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember 100 per cent, but I cannot remember the details, but I know he was there. I saw him twice in the white house 100 per cent, 100 per cent. Half his face I saw, and I am 100 per cent sure that I saw it was him, but I cannot remember in detail whether I was wrong or not, but I am sure I saw him twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Deomic, can you look carefully around the courtroom, please, and tell us if Dusko Tadic is in court today and, if so, point him out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic, yes, that is he.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where is he sitting, can you describe where he is sitting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is sitting in the middle over there, next to the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the record reflect the identification of the accused?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. The record will reflect the identification of the accused. He has pointed, of course, to Mr. Tadic but there are four people over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: OK. If there is any concern about that .....

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Ask him what he is wearing. Can you ask him what he is wearing?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was just about to do that, your Honour. Mr. Deomic, can you tell us what Mr. Tadic is wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. Can you describe what he is wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I get up?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, if you need to see.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, sir, if you need to see, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is wearing a suit, a green and white shirt, and a coloured tie, a purple-ish, blue-ish green.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Deomic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The record will reflect that the witness identified the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Nothing further, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Cross-examination, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Deomic, did you live in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have you ever lived in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I lived in Kamicani.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you were in work did you work in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What work did you do in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked for Dedo Turkanovic. I was reconstructing his summer garden, the restaurant and the coffee bar and the stage, reconstructing things, tables and things like that. Then in Kolotur in the restaurant, doing the outside walls of the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So am I right in saying then that your work in Kozarac has been of the nature of two building jobs in that town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the same company, the same men, but in two different, on two different sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because what I have to suggest to you is this, that you did not know Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did. Oh, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That you did not spend any time with Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was sitting at the same table with Dusko Tadic in Kozarac, in Basta. He was looking for a man who would help him to build this small house with the coffee bar. I was very busy because I had a lot of work already, so nothing came out of it. Then he had to look for other builders and I went on with my work in the summer garden in Basta.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So that the one occasion that you say he spoke to you in recent times would have been to ask you to do some work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I do not know how to put it. He was looking for somebody to build it for him. We were at the same table. There was Dedo there and some of the Turkanovic brothers and his best colleague, Ferid's brother-in-law, he was his best colleague, and he was a manager or ran a shoemaker's shop and they told Tadic that I was an excellent, that I was a master builder and that I said I was sorry, I was too busy and I would not have time, I would be very glad to come and help and build all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know Dusan Kuezevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had you ever seen Dusko Tadic on a motor bike before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You had never seen him in Kozarac on a motor bike?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So let us go to that time that you say you saw Dusko Tadic in Omarska. You said that he was ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- riding a motor bike?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you see him arrive on a motor bike in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was riding a motor bike, but it was not his. The motor bike belonged to another person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know whose motor bike it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who knows? No, I do not, no, but that motor bike was stolen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So how do you know it was not his motor bike?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know what every inhabitant in Kozarac had, what kind of a motor bike, what kind of a vehicle, what car, everything that everybody had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could just look at those photographs again of 239A, B and the interior photograph which is 239B, please? Thank you. Is it on the screen? If it can be put on the monitor, please. Do you see the van in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You refer to him as being near that van when you say you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not quite understand that? He was next to the van. The guard stopped him and kept him there and I was here, because this is here now. It was about a metre 20 away from the wall and I was standing here where these things are now. So one had a semicircle open, a semicircular view when the door was opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was the van there when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was by the van when he came from the direction of Omarska towards the camp, towards our camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was your door usually locked to that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes. In the beginning it was closed for a few days until things were settled with some soldiers somewhere, and then they asked to open the door so that we could breathe some air and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On this day you say that the door to the garage was open?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the door was open.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You did not actually see Dusko Tadic do anything there. Can you give us any details of anything that he did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot of course invent anything. I can only say how it was as he was coming slowly on the motor bike, and I saw him there, to the guard and the guard halted him. The van had the door opened and the guard jumped out and halted him. Then I backed away towards other people, let them breathe some air and I wanted to get as far inside as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you perhaps indicate to us where the motor bike stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here where there is this truck and this puddle, where the water is, well, behind that, behind this puddle, that is where he stopped. That is why I remember it because there were several days when there was rain and that was the puddle after that rain and the van was outside this water in the drive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This photograph was taken at the time, was it? Perhaps you cannot answer that. Can I go to the next occasion that you say you saw him which was at the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were in the room that you have pointed out to us which is the second room on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On the first occasion that you saw him, how many other people were in the room with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately 152, 53, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember 100 per cent but it is not 158. They were already leaving and God knows where they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a small room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not really. To the right and to the left were large rooms and in front in the back they were small rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A room of this size you would not normally expect to find a 150 people in, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Small rooms 150 people, incredible, no. It is only possible if they stand, but from the outside the guards do not allow it. Everybody's head had to be down, not only head, not even anyone's fingers could stick out above the window level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you sitting down there in the corner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the corner, yes, sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were the other people in the room sitting as well or were any of them standing up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all sitting down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you in that same position the second time that you say you saw Dusko Tadic in the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you sitting down again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the departure to Manjaca my place was in the corner to the right I never moved from there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On this second occasion were the numbers in the room the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: About how many were in the room at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, I cannot remember the second time how many people were there. There were less, but I cannot remember how many and we did count them. At any time when the guards were not behind the glass door or the window we counted them all and the number was decreasing. How many I cannot remember, but there were less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were there still very many people in the room, far too many than there should have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More than should have been, no, but less and less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But was the room crammed with people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. In the beginning in the white house the second door to the right, that small room, yes, at the beginning of the first day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you describe what Mr. Tadic looked like when you saw him, how he was dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot, no, I cannot remember details, but I am 100 per cent sure that I saw Tadic twice in the corridor, but the details I cannot recall those.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you remember what clothes he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No way, no, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you remember making a statement to the investigators in this case sometime ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I gave a statement that I had seen him twice 100 per cent, but I cannot remember the details what he looked like, otherwise it was when you see him once and get away from his view, hide so that he does not notice you, so that nobody raises his head or finger or hand. We had to be completely still, not a hair was allowed to move on our heads, it was that terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you remember saying he wore a blue jacket?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from the first garage. I am not positive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you were in the white house and sitting down in the corner, can you remember who else was sitting around near you at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Next to me was a Prijedor journalist. Then after the journalist I think somebody I did not know sat next to him, and then my relatives were over there beneath the window, all family of mine, all my kin, my relatives, and then there were people I did not know. They were from Prijedor and from Rakovcani. They were from all over and next to me was this Schipetar who had a sweet shop in Prijedor, who owned a sweet shop in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were they with you when you saw Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You see, what I suggest to you is that you did not see Mr. Tadic in Omarska at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did. I saw him and I confirm it 100 per cent. I did see him, I guarantee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One moment your Honour. No additional questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have a few questions, sir. I believe you testified that you were held at Benkovac for three days and two nights, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three days and two nights.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Then you were taken to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not quite understand the question. Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you taken to Omarska after those three days and two nights?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that I was taken to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were taken to Benkovac on -- do you recall what your testimony was? Was it on the second or third day after the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second day it was on. The third day we were already captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So then you would have arrived at Omarska around, if I have looked at this calendar correctly, May 26th or May 27th, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. OK. Do you remember the date that you arrived at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know it was towards the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know it was towards the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is fine. Then you were taken to the garage when you arrived at Omarska and you remained there for four weeks, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Then when you saw Mr. Tadic do you remember at what point that was during those four weeks, was it the first week, the second week, the third week or the fourth week, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember it was after the interrogation, some five or six days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were interrogated for three weeks, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I am not absolutely positive to remember days and nights, minutes, seconds. With all that horror, with all that pressure, with all the torture one cannot remember. It is impossible to say the minute or the second when something happened, but I know it was after the interrogation that I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That would have been sometime in June, I suppose, if my understanding of the dates is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Then how long after -- well, then after four weeks at Omarska you were then taken to the white house, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did you leave Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the month of August. I cannot again remember the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How long after you were taken to the white house did you see Mr. Tadic, the first time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the white house?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember those days. I cannot remember them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How long were you in the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed there until August, until I left to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So, it may have been in July or August or late June? If you do not recall that is fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you testify that you helped Mr. Tadic build his house or the top part of his house or did you testify that he had wanted you to help him build the house but that you were busy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It was the latter, that he wanted you to help him build his house and you were busy, is that what you testified to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was looking for people who would build it, but they were very busy and he came to the place where I worked, where I was doing this reconstruction of this coffee bar, of the restaurant, and they explained to him that I was really a very good builder, a real master builder, and he said he needed one like that to help him build his coffee bar. I told him I could not, I was too busy, if he could wait I could take it up later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So then you did not help him build his house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was helping a relative which was putting a roof on his house.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you. Mr. Tieger, do you have additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Mr. Deomic being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Deomic, you are permanently excused. You may leave, sir. You are free to leave. You are permanently excused. Thank you for coming. You may leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at all. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, it is 20 minutes after 5. Rather than call the next witness there are a couple of matters the Chamber wanted to talk to counsel about. First, I wanted to remind you that the Prosecutor is to file its response to the Defence's motion regarding the photograph ID spread, but I believe that you have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have some advanced copies. The official copy has been filed with the Registrar but I have some advanced copies for the Bench here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If the Usher will pick those up we will take the advance copies. Have you given one of those advance copies to Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, the Defence has already been served, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We had said that we would hear argument on this matter tomorrow afternoon. How long do you anticipate you will need, Mr. Wladimiroff, to present your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It may depend, your Honour, on the admissibility of having Dr. Wagenaar available to testify, if your Court will accept that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If we do not hear his testimony you have presented your position, but you may of course present it once again. How long would that need?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Then I will have to cover things that I expect him to tell you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If we say that we do not want to hear him, you are going to tell us what he is going to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I will try to do so, yes, and that will take a little bit more time.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: How long would it take if we allowed him to testify?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I think for him to testify will take about half an hour, that is what I think.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. If you tell us what he is going to testify about, that will take half an hour too or will there be cross-examination? OK, half an hour for Dr. Wagenaar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If he is available. I have been advised that he arrived today back home from abroad and he will call me tonight to tell me whether he is available tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then maybe half an hour for your argument for yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Who will present argument for the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, since it is taking the form of a responsive presentation, I would estimate that half an hour or so is probably an appropriate length of time for us as well, again, with the caveat that it is not entirely clear to me what the Defence intends to present.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I see in your submission, Mr. Tieger, you have cited some cases. Have you provided the Chamber with copies of those? If not, would you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If they have not been provided, your Honour, they will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: May the Defence have copies of that too?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Provide the Defence as well. I do not know what the Defence's library is like, but ours is not what it should be. So if you are giving them to us give them to the Defence as well, please. So maybe two hours. Is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I guess the only remaining question, your Honour, is how to balance the time we will devote tomorrow to the motion against the witnesses who are here. I think one of the primary concerns is that we do not end up in a position with a witness who is in the middle of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We had planned on hearing argument in the afternoon, tomorrow afternoon. I am planning on two hours and so if we start at 2.30 then we would continue. Two hours, that is 4.30. You have a witness here to offer in the morning, do you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So you have a witness for how much time now? You would need three and a half, a witness to cover maybe two and a half, maybe three hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. I do not have concerns about the morning session at all, but there are two witnesses here. My only concern is whether we begin -- I think it is just something we will have to take up at the time. I am just raising the issue now.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You have two witnesses and you probably want to know whether you should release the other witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is one solution.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that because the next witness will take how long? Do you estimate two to three hours? Mr. Niemann handled a witness in 20 minutes and he had listed the time as two to three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I do not intend to borrow Mr. Niemann's time, your Honour!

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No. I was suggesting that maybe you do the same thing. Even if you do an hour then you can do the other witness. I would suggest that you have both witnesses here, I would suggest out abundance of caution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure and we would intend to. I am only raising the issue now in case we get to a point where it is not entirely clear whether we should proceed with the second witness or not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You will have two witnesses here. That is enough time for three and a half hours, if we are going to spend two hours, is that correct? You will need three and a half hours for two witnesses or will you need maybe a third witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. Maybe I am not making my concerns clear. I think that there is certainly a possibility that we are -- I am not concerned about not having a third witness here. I do not think we will have so much time left over that there will be a problem with wasted Court time. I am just concerned about the possibility that we will have to make a decision before calling the second witness, gauging the projected amount of time he will testify or not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We want to hear as many witnesses as possible. We have three and a half hours, so we will hear one witness if it takes three and a half hours, two witnesses, three witnesses, and if that is part heard we will hear them because we want to hear as many witnesses as possible. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It sounds like the issue is raised here, so that is a concern, would want to truncate a witness's testimony for a two and a half to a three-week period?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not know. We will play it by ear. You have enough witnesses here to use up three and a half hours, OK, and then we will see. I just do not want us to be sitting here without a witness. OK? Will you have witnesses here to spend three and a half hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We will have two witnesses here, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not know how long they are going to take, that is the problem, Mr. Tieger. All I can say is you have three and a half hours tomorrow, use it, please. OK? Mr. Wladimiroff, you will have your decision on your protective measures tomorrow. The other matter I have been asked to ask you, Mr. Wladimiroff, regarding video conferencing where you would propose to offer the witnesses, you need the not tell me at this time, but that is a concern that the technical people need to know, because it has to do with the equipment that is necessary. I did not speak with you, Miss Featherstone about this. Perhaps you could spend a moment with Mr. Wladimiroff to see if you can discuss this and then we will give that information to the appropriate person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We have been discussing this morning with the technical unit and I am aware we have to solve this problem.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. We will then adjourn until tomorrow at 10 o'clock. (5.30 p.m.) (The court adjourned until the following day). 19
